intro:
Use it to show that an app is hearing someone, or that someone is speaking: over a microphone button, in a recording row, beside each person on a call, or behind a whole voice screen.

It draws a level and does not record one. Pass it a microphone, a call or an audio element as `source` and it measures the sound itself, or pass a `level` from 0 to 1 that you measure. `useMicrophone` asks for the microphone and gives you the stream.

With no level it runs its own motion for the current `state`, which is enough to build and review a voice screen before any audio exists.

For a spinner while an answer is being written, use a loader. For a recording's length and position alone, a progress bar is clearer.
usage:
const mic = useMicrophone()

<Soundwave variant="dots" source={mic.stream} />
<Button onClick={mic.toggle}>{mic.active ? 'Stop' : 'Speak'}</Button>

<Soundwave variant="radial" state="speaking">
  <Soundwave.Center>
    <Avatar name="Khalid Abdi" size="xl" />
  </Soundwave.Center>
</Soundwave>

parts.Center: What sits in the middle of a `radial` or `ring` wave, such as an avatar or a figure. It is sized to the hole and centred in it. The other looks have no middle and do not use it.

examples.title: Capsules
examples.description: A few large capsules, for the space above a microphone button. Each capsule moves at its own pace and the middle ones lead, so the group follows one level without moving as a block.

examples.title: Metering bars
examples.description: `static` gives every bar a share of the current level, for a live meter. `scrolling` keeps a history that slides left with the newest sample at the right edge, for a recording in progress. `centered={false}` grows the bars up from the bottom.

examples.title: Travelling wave
examples.description: One line, tapered to nothing at both ends so it meets the edges flat. Use it while an assistant is speaking.

examples.title: A field of dots
examples.description: `dots` lights a grid of dots into a wave, column by column. Unlit dots stay faintly visible, so the field keeps its shape when the voice is quiet. It takes `static`, `scrolling` and `levels`, as `bars` does.

examples.title: Spokes round a person
examples.description: `radial` draws spokes round a ring, with `Soundwave.Center` in the middle for an avatar. `height` is the diameter. Each spoke is solid near the ring and fainter at its tip, and a glow behind it grows with the level.

examples.title: A conversation
examples.description: One `radial` wave per person, in the same colour as their avatar. The person speaking gets `state="speaking"` and the others `idle`, which leaves them short spokes rather than nothing, so everyone on the call stays visible. In an app, pass each person's own stream as `source`; here the microphone speaks for Khalid.

examples.title: Rings of dots
examples.description: `ring` lights rings of dots outward from the middle, one reach for each angle. Given `levels` it draws them still: here one value for each hour of a day, read clockwise from midnight at the top. With a `source` or a `level` it moves like the other looks, which the microphone button shows.

examples.title: States
examples.description: With no `level`, `state` picks the motion: `idle` barely moves, `listening` and `speaking` run several waves at unrelated speeds, and `thinking` is slower and shallower. `state` also sets what a screen reader announces, whether or not a level is passed.

examples.title: Your own audio
examples.description: `source` takes the sound itself: the `stream` from `useMicrophone`, a `MediaStream` from a call, or an `<audio>` or `<video>` element. The wave measures it on every frame and nothing re-renders. Keep the element in state rather than a ref, so the wave hears about it once it has mounted.

examples.title: A voice note
examples.description: `levels` is the shape of a finished recording: sample `mic.level.current` while recording and keep the numbers beside the file, rather than decoding the audio to draw it. With `levels` the wave is still, and `progress` is the playhead: bars behind it keep full ink and the rest are dimmed. Press the microphone to record a note of your own, then play it back.

examples.title: Colours
examples.description: `color` takes a role from the theme. Left unset, the wave is drawn in the text colour of whatever contains it. `trackColor` sets the unlit dots of `dots` and `ring`, and the unplayed part of a recording. `gradient` spreads several roles across a strip.

examples.title: Ambient glow
examples.description: `ambient` fills its nearest positioned parent with a glow rising from the bottom edge and a rim of light round the rest, both growing with the level. It takes no pointer events, so put it behind the content. It defaults to `info`, since a glow in the text colour reads as a shadow.

notes:
### Sound in

There are three ways to give the wave something to draw, from least work to most control.

- **`source`**: a `MediaStream` or an `<audio>` or `<video>` element. The wave measures it with the browser's audio analyser on every frame. A media file has to be on the same site or sent with CORS headers (`crossOrigin="anonymous"` on the element); otherwise the browser hides its sound from the page and the wave stays still.
- **`useMicrophone()`**: asks for the microphone on `start`, which has to be called from a click, and gives back `stream` for `source`, a `level` ref, a `status` and `stop`. The microphone is released on `stop` and when the component unmounts. A refused permission or a missing microphone sets `status` to `denied`.
- **`level`**: a number from 0 to 1, or a ref holding one. `useAudioLevel(source)` returns such a ref, for when the reading is needed elsewhere too, such as to keep a recording's shape. Use a plain number for something slow, such as a speaking flag from a server.

With none of them the wave runs its own motion for `state`, so a screen can be built before any audio exists.

The level is smoothed with a fast rise and a slow fall, so the wave jumps on a syllable and settles gently instead of flickering on every sample. `sensitivity` multiplies it before it is capped at 1, for a quiet source; `useMicrophone({ floor: -45 })` ignores more of a noisy room.

### Drawing

Each look is one or two SVG paths, and every dot is a round end on a line of no length, so a field of several hundred dots is a single path. Each frame rewrites those paths and changes no React state.

The strips (`bars`, `line` and `dots`) take the width of their container, so give the container a width. `pills`, `radial` and `ring` size themselves from their props.

### When it stops

The wave stops drawing when it is scrolled out of view or its tab is hidden, and starts again when it comes back. `paused` holds the current frame. With reduced motion turned on, the wave holds a still frame instead of moving.

A wave with `levels` and no `scrolling` never animates, so a list of twenty voice notes costs nothing until one plays.

### Screen readers

The wave is one image, announced by its state ("Listening"). Pass `label` to say more, such as who is speaking. What is inside `Soundwave.Center` is part of that image and is not read separately.
